I run about forty senior interviews a year, and the plan question is where I learn the most. Here is what I hear from a weak candidate. The whole answer comes back in will. I will meet the team, I will review the roadmap, I will build a plan. Every sentence is correct English, and the whole thing still sounds like it was invented in the last ninety seconds, because will is the form you use when you decide while you are speaking. Now here is the strong version. Some of it comes back as going to, which tells me the decision existed before I asked the question. I am going to spend the first two weeks with the engineering leads. Some of it comes back in the present continuous, with a date attached, which tells me it is already arranged and other people are already holding that time. And somewhere in the middle, the candidate names the headwind. That is the one thing I ask everybody for. Tell me what is going to make this plan harder, and tell me before I have to ask.

Hi, this is the short version of the January plan, so you do not have to read the whole deck. First, the calendar. I am presenting the plan to the steering group on the fourteenth of January, and that meeting is already booked, so please send me your numbers before the tenth. Second, the decision we have already made. We are going to sunset the legacy platform, and the date is March. That is not a proposal any more, it is in the plan, so please stop building new reports on top of it. Third, the part I am not committing to yet. I want a two-week reporting cadence, and I know some of you want it tomorrow, but I will only commit to it once the baseline exists. Take the baseline in week one, and as soon as I can see the trajectory, I will confirm the rhythm. Last thing. My honest forecast is that hiring is going to be our biggest headwind this year, so if you can pull one quick win forward into February, do it.
